column2: tradeoff
Three-phase commit keeps every replica in sync, but push latency is bound by the slowest replica, so adding replicas for read capacity worsens write throughput.
column5: performance efficiency (write latency and throughput); scalability of replica count

column2: A minimum of three replicas per repository is required for safety, which wastes resources on the many small, mostly idle repositories that agents create.
column5: cost (storage and replicas for idle repositories)

column2: Writes that cannot be committed to at least two replicas are refused: durability and consistency are kept at the price of write availability during failures.
Git clients and CI need strongly consistent repositories, so eventual consistency is rejected and the system pays a high complexity cost to stay fully consistent.
column4: functional suitability (correctness seen by Git clients); reliability (consistency)

column2: Making the replicas on disk the source of truth turns every repository into a pet: a routing database, constant checksums and fast repair are needed, and two corrupt copies block pushes.
column4: reliability (consistency through quorum of disk replicas)
column5: maintainability (operability); reliability (availability depends on routing database)

column2: Pushes are acknowledged only once persisted in the S3 write-ahead log, so push throughput is capped by S3 write latency, mitigated by batching and a faster storage class.
Only the primary compacts and replicas download the compacted packs, trading network bandwidth for CPU and avoiding failovers caused by repacking on every replica.
column4: performance efficiency (CPU use); reliability (availability during maintenance)

column2: Any node may act as primary because WAL updates use compare-and-swap on S3; this keeps the system correct during failovers, but a non-preferred primary causes CAS retries that delay pushes.
column4: reliability (fault tolerance and correctness when degraded)

column2: Repositories on disk are a cache rematerialized from the WAL, which removes routing tables and lets idle replicas be dropped, at the cost of materialization work when a repository is missing.
column4: maintainability (operability without routing state); cost (no replicas for idle repositories)
column5: performance efficiency (latency and work of rematerializing)

column2: Storing packfiles in blob storage and references in a relational database scales well for large reference transactions, but requires operating a relational database alongside the blob store.
column5: maintainability (operating an external database); reliability (consistency across two stores)

column2: Distributing the filesystem kept Git and the Rails application unchanged, but networked and block-replicated filesystems were slow, buggy and hard to operate.
column4: maintainability (no application or Git changes); cost (development effort)
column5: performance efficiency (random packfile reads over the network); maintainability (operability)

column2: Moving repositories to dedicated fileservers behind an RPC layer gave horizontal scalability, but each repository still had a single copy, so availability and hot-repository performance did not improve.
Storing Git objects in a distributed hash table scales storage out, but graph walks need a round trip per object and the protocol still requires packfiles, making clones too slow.
Placing replicas far apart improves disaster survival and lets reads go to a nearby replica, but each reference update needs several long round trips.
column4: reliability (durability against regional disasters); performance efficiency (read latency)

column2: Detecting failed servers from real application traffic is faster and catches subtle failures, but sometimes marks healthy servers offline.
Quiescing a server before a reboot lets long reads such as clones finish, but maintenance can take hours instead of seconds.

The GVFS protocol downloads only commits and trees and fetches objects on demand, cutting transfer for huge repositories, but couples clients to a central server, a custom Git and co-located cache servers.
column4: performance efficiency (data transfer and clone size)
column5: portability (custom Git and host-specific protocol); cost (cache-server infrastructure)

column2: Replacing the virtualized filesystem with sparse-checkout keeps standard Git, but checkout is slower than with VFS for Git, which could defer populating files.
Running maintenance incrementally in the background instead of foreground auto-GC keeps commands responsive; simply disabling GC would let performance decay.
Sparse-checkout lets developers populate only a fraction of the repository, but the repository must be designed for it and users must request more directories.
